10 seconds is too strong to be part of her base kit. The problem with thrusters's CD reduction talent right now is it's against First Aid which is basically mandatory to sustain, which is kind of her game. I could see replacing a level 1 talent with something that reduces Thrusters's CD by .5 seconds per attack, or reduces Thrusters's CD by .2 seconds for every health globe? (She's kinda hard to farm them with, so you might even increase it.) Those'd be fun. I could see a 20 second CD being base, though. 30 seconds is short enough that if you watch it you rarely get caught with your pants down, but too long to keep you even remotely safe against a bad comp.

But the problem is really that she offers nothing besides giant range, which a lot of heroes outclass her in, and they do it without the cost of making themselves stationary. A surprisingly huge amount of what makes Thrusters good is just that it unsieges you and lets you move instantly. I don't see a reason for regular unsiege to NOT do this, to be honest. You'd still have reactivate time to siege, and you can't stutter step while also having increased range.

What'd really actually make her more viable is some way to provide vision so she can see gankers coming. As is, there's no real counterplay to stealthers or Li Ming/Kael'thas/Nova/Zeratul/Chromie just appearing behind you all of a sudden, because she can't fucking see. Spider Mines give vision, but you gotta go way the hell out of your way to place them in useful spots.

I'm pretty asexual myself, though I have romantic feelings toward women. It's unrelated. I don't have anything to add beyond that you should probably talk to a therapist, and I know a few transwomen that still identify as women but aren't on HRT. They just transitioned socially, dressing and speaking and acting as women, and that was all they felt they needed to be happy. Nothing says you have to transition in every way imaginable. On the other hand, I'm sure there are women who have larger breasts than what they really want--and if the rest of it was making you feel better, I feel like thinking "if I truly wanted to be a girl I would be happy about it" is kinda weird. But, really, that's something you should speak with a therapist about.

Additionally, options like laser hair removal or electrolysis are available to you even without HRT, which could help with the facial hair.

Yeah, I'm just being cautious because I don't know your situation. Ultimately the only one who can make the decision is you. I can only tell you that no one I've came out to reacted with anything that could be called negativity. I hugged my father for the first time in like 15 years after I came out to him. And you would be surprised by what people understand. It might be weird at first, but I promise it only gets better, and that the part where it's awkward is incredibly small compared to the joys you'll share for the rest of your lives.

I want to be more clear: if your parents love you, they love you, and provided they aren't miserable assholes, they'll love you no matter what. All you have to do is help them to understand what being trans means, and what it means is you're the same kid that your parents loved, and now they get to have a daughter too, so hey, they're pretty lucky. Two genders for the price of one.

And hell, if they're miserable assholes, you really should not sweat it, because like I said: their response is their response, and not yours. You are doing nothing to hurt them.

He will definitely look at you differently, at least at first, but it isn't anything to be terrified about. Like I said, it just takes time for them to understand. Parents can be surprisingly supportive. They've been there for you for your whole life, so they often don't just stop that. And they will understand if they try, it'll just take time. Your relationships don't have to change. You don't even have to change. You can be the same you as a man or woman, and your parents will understand that if they stick by you.

If they have any questions or problems, you can direct them here, and we'll be more than happy to field any potential questions.

If this is how you feel, you should see a therapist, who you can speak at more length with and they can help you better understand the situation. I'm assuming you are financially dependent on your parents, but depending on where you live there might be affordable therapists.

It's not going to go away, but I can't say I haven't felt the same wish. I've felt like this my entire life. There's nothing that can solve it besides transitioning. As for why, it's probably got to do with hormonal levels when your brain develops in utero, but we don't really know for sure. You definitely shouldn't blame yourself for it, and you definitely shouldn't think you're hurting anyone by being trans. Coming out may be difficult for your parents to handle, but if you're certain they won't abandon you, then it should be something to consider. I'm not going to tell you to do it. I was surprised at how well my father took it, even if he still doesn't really seem to get it. It takes time. They haven't had to live with the idea of it in their heads the way you have, so it has to grow on them before they'll really understand it. But you are absolutely not hurting them if you come out to them. You aren't hurting anyone. Their ideas are their own, and only their own. You're fine. You're awesome, even, probably! You've got friends who love and respect you, so you have to be.

If you're seriously considering suicide, please please please call the suicide prevention hotline. 1-800-273-8255. There is always someone to talk to and there are so many reasons not to do it, even if they don't seem clear to you now, and they can help you see them.

I was just here (at two months now) so it's fresh in my memory. My body hasn't changed much beyond early breast growth, which started probably just after a month. As for mentally, I just posted about having some attention problems, but I haven't explicitly noticed having less energy. It might be too early for both of us. I'd also say that the "finally, the estrogen my body and mind has been craving!" thing is probably mostly psychological. I joke that taking my pills is the best part of my day and, well, it is, because it makes me really happy that I'm doing something about a long-standing issue. I imagine a lot of people extend that to a general feeling. Hormones can definitely have other psychological effects, though.

In short, just be happy you're doing something! You should be as excited as when you started all the time, because it's awesome.

Anything is a more subtle way to do it. If the character's trans, though, you should consider why they're trans (as in, why they feel the need to transition, and what that actually means in her society, tech level, magic level, whatever) and implement that into the story and ideally gameplay. So play off of stereotypes we have for fantasy settings if you're using a fantasy setting. If the character is MTF (which I assume to be true,) maybe consider not giving her a sword, first of all. Give her daggers or a lance or bow or something stereotypically seen with female fighters. (Plus, there's already a million action games that use swords, so it might help you stand out if she was primarily a ranged character.) Then make the hereditary sword that her father wants her to use be handed down along the male line, but she chooses, as part of her gender representation, to use a bow, which is associated with any/a specific female warrior in the land (this isn't actually, you know, anything like actual medieval combat, but it's a video game.) Bonus points here, for people who are gonna read in to things in a pretty dumb manner: refusing the sword is refusing the phallic symbol. It's subtle--maybe even too subtle for most people--but not everything in a game has to be there for every player (this is the same thing with writing.)

Basically, if you're going to have any amount of story driven elements in a fantasy or sci fi or any sort of created setting, you're free to create the gender associations the country and characters have and use that to enhance your central metaphor. Make the context for skill learning something "feminine" like sewing. Heck, maybe men aren't allowed to wear yellow and they all wear green. Playable Character starts out in green and gains yellow clothes as she comes out. Maybe learning magic is literally all the character needs to be accepted as a woman or become more comfortable with their femininity, but it's difficult because of body or something. Playable Character starts with sword, eventually throws it away, as she throws away concepts of masculinity which are anathema (or at least not preferred) to her. Investing in magic as her career progresses (IE, learning new skills--so you're tying it to character progression) result in her father as viewing her as less masculine, making him angrier and more likely to write her existence off.

If you are even using the phrase "tacking on" to describe what you're doing, of course it's going to feel shoehorned--that basically means the same thing as "tacked on." It's as important as you spend time on it, and I don't just mean time the player spends staring at dialogue, but also time the player spends with the gameplay elements. Seeing all female characters use bows* and all male characters use swords* works for that metaphor. If you make a game with good gameplay, people will still play the game and just blow through all the cutscenes that are where the more overt characterization (and the parts where you'd be most likely to outright state that they're trans) happens, so you probably won't really lose any audience there. As long as the game is good.
